Back-translation: "I am allergic to ___." Masculine speaker (file convention); a woman says "Soy alérgica a ___" (ah-LEHR-hee-kah). a + el contracts to al (al gluten, al maní), so the article goes with the word, not the frame. Safety item: please verify. Word notes: peanuts = "maní" (most of Latin America), "cacahuate" (Mexico), "cacahuete" (Spain). Nuts = "frutos secos" (tree nuts generally); "nueces" strictly means walnuts but is used loosely in Mexico. Back-translations of examples: "I am allergic to the nuts / the peanut / the gluten / the shellfish / the milk / the eggs" (Spanish uses the article here). Dairy = "los lácteos". [Fixed 2026-10-14 per ChatGPT review.]
Masculine speaker; a woman says "Soy vegetariana".

Uses tú like the rest of the file. Asking a shop, café or hotel (the business), "¿Tienen ___?" (TYEH-nen, plural) is the most natural; usted form is "¿Tiene ___?". The blank takes an article only when English has one (wifi, comida vegetariana, but un cargador, un mapa), so the article goes with the word.
Blank takes the word with its article (un café, la habitación). Plural nouns need "¿Cuánto cuestan ___?". "¿Cuánto es?" is also common at the till.

Back-translation: "I need ___, please." Blank takes the word with its article when English has one (un taxi; ayuda and agua take none). Safety item: please verify. Help example back-translates as "I need help, please."; in a real emergency people shout "¡Ayuda!" or "¡Socorro!" instead. The doctor variant reuses the existing need_doctor phrase.

Blank takes un/una with the word (un baño, una farmacia), so the article is part of the blank. "Por aquí" (por ah-KEE) instead of "cerca" is equally common. Bathroom: "baño" in Latin America; Spain says "aseo" or "servicio" in public places.
The preposition changes with the filler, so it is inside the blank: cash is "en efectivo" (con efectivo is heard but less standard), card and phone take "con" (con tarjeta, con el teléfono).
Uses tú like the rest of the file (usted: "¿Puede ___?"). Object pronouns attach to the verb (escribirlo) or move before puedes ("¿Me lo puedes escribir?"), both natural.

First blank takes un/una with the item (un café, un té, agua with no article); the noun after sin drops its article (sin leche). Coffee without milk is often ordered as "un café solo" (Spain) or "un café negro / americano" (Latin America).

Blank takes an infinitive phrase. Regional verbs: park = "estacionar" (Latin America), "aparcar" (Spain); take photos = "tomar fotos" (Latin America), "hacer/sacar fotos" (Spain). For a seat, "¿Está libre?" (is it free?) is also very common.
Blank takes the word with its article or possessive (mi hotel, la entrada, un restaurante). "Busco ___" (BOOS-koh) is shorter and equally correct.

Incluido agrees with the noun, so the frame is only literal for masculine singular words: feminine "¿Está incluida la propina?", plural "¿Están incluidos los impuestos?". Blank takes the word with its article (el desayuno). Tax: "los impuestos" is general; Spain and Mexico usually say "el IVA".

Blank takes an infinitive phrase. Regional: get a taxi = "tomar un taxi" (Latin America), "coger un taxi" (Spain; avoid coger in Mexico/Argentina); tickets = "boletos" (Latin America), "billetes"/"entradas" (Spain; entradas for shows/museums).
Said to someone you are flirting with; both gender forms are shown where the language changes with who you talk to.

l2_seven_evening.target: Empieza a las siete de la tarde.
l2_seven_evening.pronunciation_easy: em-PYEH-sah ah las SYEH-teh deh lah TAR-deh
l2_seven_evening.qa: Seven is "de la tarde" in Spain, "de la noche" in much of Latin America.
